title: Broomfield Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Broomfield wells have a 62 ft median depth, but records range to 1,581 ft. See yield, water levels, costs and local risks.
h1: What Broomfield Well Records Mean for a Property
intro_html:
Well records around Broomfield show a wide range of drilling conditions. The median reported depth is 62 feet, but the middle half runs from 25 to 390 feet, and the deepest recorded well reaches 1,581 feet. That spread matters when you are pricing a lot, comparing neighboring properties, or reviewing a driller’s proposal.

The records include 3,129 wells in Colorado Division of Water Resources permit data, though only 1,459 are recorded as constructed. Yield and water-level data are also incomplete, so these figures describe the local pattern rather than guaranteeing what a new well will produce.

sections.heading: Broomfield well depths vary sharply across the Denver Basin
sections.html:
More than half of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, which explains the low median. That does not make a shallow well a safe assumption for every parcel. Another 12% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 18% between 300 and 600 feet, and 16% exceed 600 feet.

Broomfield sits over Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, while permits also identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock water sources, Laramie Fox Hills, and alluvial aquifers. Local geology, the targeted aquifer, casing and grout requirements, and the exact lot can all change the bid. Use nearby wells in Broomfield first, then compare records from Lafayette, Northglenn, Louisville, Westminster, Superior, and Erie rather than relying on the median alone.

sections.heading: What Broomfield wells produce for household use
sections.html:
Among the 276 wells with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half falls from 7.5 to 13.0 gallons per minute, and 74% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable production range for ordinary household use when the well, pressure system, storage, and legal use all match the property.

Low-yield records still matter: 4% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 6% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Ask for the well test, not just a permit. A yield result does not by itself establish water quality or the legal ability to add irrigation, livestock, or additional household uses. DWR records also include monitoring wells, so not every record represents a domestic supply.

sections.heading: Broomfield water levels and the recent record
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median of 14 feet below ground, with the middle half between 10 and 44 feet. That describes the water level when measured under static conditions, not the level while a pump is running. A driller still needs to evaluate drawdown, recovery, and the proposed pump setting for the particular well.

The decade comparison does not show a simple dropping pattern in these records. The median measured level was 25 feet below surface in the 2010s and 11 feet in the 2020s. Different wells, locations, aquifers, and measurement conditions can explain that difference, so it should not be treated as proof of a basin-wide rise or decline. Only 111 wells report a static water level, which limits how broadly the trend can be applied.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Broomfield, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity spans decades. Records show 66 permits from the 1950s, 75 from the 1960s, 299 from the 1970s, 237 from the 1980s, 565 from the 1990s, 393 from the 2000s, 349 from the 2010s, and 293 from the 2020s. The newest permit year in the data is 2025.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 715 wells, Waneka & Son Drilling with 246, and John'S Drilling Inc. with 126. Those counts are record history, not endorsements or current availability. Check the permit, construction report, pump test, and current licensing before selecting a driller. A DWR permit is also not the same thing as a completed, producing well.

sections.heading: A Broomfield drilling budget starts with depth
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 62-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models at about $3,100 to $4,300. That is a starting estimate, not a complete water system price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,100 to $16,300 at that median depth. A parcel requiring several hundred feet, special casing or grout, difficult access, or a different completion can move well beyond that range. Request a written bid that separates drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work. Do not use the shallow median to budget a lot whose nearby wells are substantially deeper.

sections.heading: Broomfield risks to investigate before closing
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve attention because depth and production vary widely. Ask for neighboring construction reports, pump tests, static levels, and any failed or abandoned well records. Fractured-bedrock production can be unpredictable, and a nearby productive well does not guarantee the same result on your parcel.

Water quality also needs testing. Within about 10 miles, the mapped data includes 595 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 26 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, and 98 historic mine features. These mapped sites do not prove contamination at a specific property, but they are reasons to test the raw well water for contaminants relevant to the site history. Confirm septic setbacks, usable building area, access for a drill rig, and the location of casing, grout, pump equipment, and electrical service before finalizing a building plan.

sections.heading: A practical Broomfield lot review
sections.html:
For an existing home, obtain the well permit, construction report, pump information, recent water test, and service history before relying on the listing description. Confirm the well’s permitted use. In Colorado, an exempt household-use well is subject to specific limits, including the 35-gallon-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit, and additional uses may require different rights or an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin.

For vacant land, start with the closest comparable wells in Broomfield and nearby Lafayette, Northglenn, Louisville, Westminster, Superior, or Erie. Have a licensed driller assess access, likely depth, aquifer target, casing and grout, and pump design. Coordinate the well with septic and the house footprint before excavation. A strong purchase decision is based on a feasible water plan, not simply the presence of a permit on the map.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Broomfield?
faq.a: The median reported well depth around Broomfield is 62 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 25 to 390 feet, while the 90th percentile is 858 feet and the deepest record is 1,581 feet. Depth varies with the targeted Denver Basin or other aquifer, the parcel’s geology, and the nearby well pattern.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Broomfield?
faq.a: The local model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 62-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $3,100 to $4,300. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical models at about $9,100 to $16,300. A deeper well, difficult access, or special construction can increase the actual bid.

faq.q: How much water do Broomfield wells produce?
faq.a: Among 276 records with a reported pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 7.5 to 13.0 gallons per minute. Seventy-four percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Production is not guaranteed, and a pump test is more useful for a specific property than the area median.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Broomfield?
faq.a: Well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Test the water from the specific well before relying on it. Within about 10 miles, mapped data includes 595 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 26 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a property is contaminated, but they support site-specific testing and review of local land-use history.

faq.q: Are Broomfield well water levels going down?
faq.a: The available record does not show a simple decline. Median measured depth to water was 25 feet below surface in the 2010s and 11 feet in the 2020s. Only 111 wells report static water levels, and the wells and measurement conditions differ. Treat the comparison as limited context, then review the closest wells and obtain a current measurement.
